title: wikicc — Architecture
html:
wikicc — Architecture

This document describes how wikicc is built: its layers, the direction of their dependencies, the invariants the stages must keep, and the constraints that shape them. It deliberately stays at that level — product behaviour is described in README.md, and per-stage implementation details live in the code.

1. Shape of the system

wikicc is one Rust binary plus one embedded front-end bundle. The binary owns everything that can be decided at build time; the bundle owns everything that has to happen in the reader. They communicate through exactly one channel: a JSON payload embedded in the page.

            build time                        │        run time
                                              │
  input dir ──▶ pipeline stages ──▶ artifact  │  artifact ──▶ reader modules
  (Rust: scan, parse, resolve,                 │  (ES modules bundled by
   assemble, render, write)                    │   esbuild, inlined as one
                                              │   classic script)
                              payload (JSON) ─┼─▶

Nothing is resolved at run time across the boundary: the bundle knows its imports when it is built, and the payload is already on the page when the script runs. There is no server in either half.

2. Pipeline

scan ──▶ parse ──▶ resolve ──▶ assemble ──▶ render ──▶ write
 .md      HTML +     link/asset   SiteBundle   page or    3 formats
 files    TOC +      rewriting,   (JSON)       page +     via
          highlight  asset bytes               chunks     SiteWriter

pipeline::run owns the order and the side effects:

StageInput → outputModule
validateraw arguments + .wikicc.json → merged, guarded Optionscli, options, config
configinput root → optional .wikicc.json → SiteConfigconfig
scandirectory + Options.exclude → ScanReportscan
parseSourceDoc → HTML, TOC, plain textmarkdown
resolvedestinations → final addressing, AssetTable, diagnosticsmarkdown::links, assets
assembleeverything → SiteBundle + SiteBuildsite
renderSiteBundle → the shell page, or the shell plus one chunk per document and the search corpusrender
writeRenderedOutput + SiteBuild → fileswriters

Every stage except write is a pure transformation over immutable data, so it is unit tested without a filesystem. The order of the side effects is part of the contract: diagnostics are reported first, then the --strict gate runs, and only then is the page rendered and written. A build that fails on warnings therefore neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one.

3. Module map

src/main.rs                 binary: parse arguments, dispatch --init-config, run the pipeline,
                            map errors to exit codes
src/lib.rs                  library root and re-exports
src/cli.rs                  clap definitions
src/options.rs              the shared Settings of the CLI and the configuration file,
                            the CLI-over-file merge, defaults, path guards
src/error.rs                error type and exit-code mapping
src/pipeline.rs             stage order, strict gate, summary lines
src/scan.rs                 discovery, ordering, ids, titles, diagnostics
src/config.rs               the optional `.wikicc.json` site configuration and its initializer
src/markdown/               render orchestration, heading text, slugs, TOC, chapter blocks,
                            highlighting, link resolution, reference definitions
src/assets.rs               read, MIME, hashing, dedupe
src/site.rs                 payload types and assembly
src/render.rs               shell assembly (template, CSS, script, payload), size guard
src/writers/                one writer per format plus the shared placeholder expansion
src/web/                    page template, stylesheet and the reader's ES modules
build.rs                    bundles src/web/js/main.js with esbuild into OUT_DIR,
                            and embeds docs/logo.ico into the Windows executable
tools/make-icon.mjs         packs the rendered icon sizes into docs/logo.ico

Dependency direction is one-way: cli → options → scan → markdown → site → render → writers → pipeline. config reads only its own file and imports options (the shared Settings) and scan (the diagnostic type), so it feeds the scan without anything reaching back into it. markdown::links never depends on site, so link resolution stays testable on its own.

4. Invariants

  1. Rewrite the tree, not the HTML. Every document is parsed once with markdown-rs into mdast, converted to the own-layer tree, and passed through the own-layer transforms (citation fold, wikilinks, inline sugar, lenient spaced destinations, callouts) before the serialiser runs. Link and image destinations are rewritten structurally while that serialiser emits elements. Regex post-processing of HTML is rejected because attribute quoting and nesting make it unsound.
  2. One page, two addressing schemes. The document HTML is rendered once and carries an opaque placeholder (wikicc-asset:<hash>) wherever a local resource is referenced. Writers expand the placeholder into the addressing form of their format. The placeholder only ever appears inside the JSON payload, and every substitution value is quote-free, so the payload stays valid JSON.
  3. The shell formats inline the payload; the pages format fetches. single-html and html-dir must work over file://, where fetch() of a local JSON file is blocked by CORS, so their whole payload is embedded in the page. pages is an artifact for an HTTP host: its page embeds only the manifest — one {id, title, hash} reference per document — and each document's model is one JSON file under pages/ that the reader fetches when it navigates there, with the search corpus in search.json fetched on the first global search. That format does not open from file://, and the reader says so when it finds itself there. Chunk file names derive from the document id alone, so a cached page never points at a file a redeploy removed; freshness travels in the hash, appended as a ?v= query a static host ignores but a browser counts as a new address.
  4. Assets are content-addressed. The name is the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 digest plus the original extension, which gives free deduplication and stable names across builds and platforms.
  5. Fail soft by default. Broken links and missing assets become warnings and the original destination is left untouched; --strict upgrades them to a non-zero exit.
  6. Raw HTML passes through unchanged. The input is trusted (a local documentation folder); there is no sanitizer in this version, and this is documented rather than half-implemented.
  7. A block ends at the next heading of any level. Each body is cut into blocks — one per heading, ending where the next heading of any level starts — so every paragraph is serialised exactly once. The outline is carried on the blocks themselves (parent, subtree), which keeps aggregation a lookup rather than a walk without repeating a paragraph under every ancestor. tests/e2e.rs asserts both halves: joining a root subtree reproduces doc.html exactly, and block markup costs one body copy however deep the outline goes.
  8. Heading text has one implementation. Anchors are matched during resolution, before the target document is rendered, so the pre-pass and the renderer build heading text through the same HeadingText accumulator and the same Slugger. A chapter the build accepts is therefore a chapter the reader can reach, and the route carries the emitted slug, since only that is an element id.
  9. Static state travels in the markup. Anything the reader must know about a link that the route grammar cannot express is written into the document as data-* attributes, and every consumer reads it from there. The mark goes on an inline <span hidden> immediately before the link — the shape that stays valid inside a paragraph, a list item or a table cell, and the one the reader copies onto the anchor it points at.

5. Determinism

Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts. This is a hard requirement, not an aspiration, and it constrains every stage:

  • documents are ordered by relative path in byte order;
  • collections that reach the output are BTreeMap/BTreeSet or explicitly sorted;
  • assets are named after their content hash, so duplicates collapse and names do not depend on discovery order;
  • no artifact contains a timestamp, an absolute path, a host name or a random value. The elapsed time exists only in the stdout summary;
  • on the front end, the force layout is seeded from a hash of the document ids, the same generator feeds the initial jitter and simulation.randomSource(), and the simulation is stepped synchronously.

6. Contracts at the edges

These are the boundaries where an internal change becomes observable, so each one is stated as a contract rather than left to the implementation.

  • The configuration file. .wikicc.json sits in the input folder root and is optional. It carries six keys — home, exclude, out, format, title, strict — exactly the Settings shape the command line also expresses, and every value it names is a default the command line overrides. A relative out is resolved against the input folder (the folder the file sits in), so the build lands in the same place whatever the working directory. The file is read once, before the scan (the exclude entries must be in effect while the tree is walked; resolving home still waits for the document ids), and parsing is strict: an unreadable or unparseable file is a runtime failure, while a home that matches no document and an unknown key are warnings the --strict gate counts. The resolved id travels in the payload as home and in the pages manifest under the same key, omitted when unset, so a site without the file serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of it. exclude lists directories relative to the input folder that are pruned with their subtrees; the pruned directories are reported as a note line, and an entry that escapes the input folder is a runtime failure, whatever the source it came from. A starter file is written by wikicc --init-config [DIR]: the default content (every key unset) goes into a directory that already exists, and a file that is already there is never overwritten.
  • CLI surface. cli defines the arguments; options owns the shared Settings (the shape both the command line and the configuration file express), merges the command line over the file over the built-in defaults into Options, and owns the output-directory guards (missing and empty are used, a previous artifact is emptied, anything else needs --force, and the output directory may not be the input root, its ancestor or the working directory). Three combinations are rejected before anything is written. --home and a repeatable --exclude replace the configured values, and --strict is three-state: a bare flag turns the gate on, --strict=false turns it off.
  • Exit codes. error maps every failure to 0 (success, possibly with warnings), 1 (runtime failure, including --strict with warnings) or 2 (usage error, reported by clap). The mapping is centralised so a new stage cannot invent a code.
  • Streams. Diagnostics go to stderr, the summary line to stdout (unless --quiet). The summary names counts, output directory, format and elapsed time — never a value that ends up inside an artifact.
  • Testability. Everything the run prints goes through a std::io::Write sink rather than println!, so wording, gate and --quiet are unit tested without spawning a process.
  • Formats. The three writers never re-render markup: the two shell writers share the page and differ only in asset addressing, and the pages writer expands the same placeholders into its chunk files. A writer receives the render of its own format and refuses any other. The pages writer expands every chunk before it writes anything, writes the shell page last, so the artifact never references a file that is not on disk, and an asset-free or document-free site writes no empty directory.
  • Weight. render.rs holds a size guard that fails the build if the bundle regresses.
  • The Windows icon. A Windows executable shows an icon in the file explorer, and that icon lives in the PE resource section. docs/logo.svg is the design source; docs/logo.ico is rendered from it and committed, so the build needs no image toolchain and stays reproducible. build.rs compiles the icon into the executable for Windows targets only, and every other target produces exactly the binary it produced before. The icon is the only thing the resource section carries, and the program keeps its console subsystem: the CLI writes to stdout and stderr as before.

7. Front end

  • Build chain. The reader is native ES modules under src/web/js, importing the engines by bare specifier. build.rs runs the npm-installed esbuild over main.js and stages one minified IIFE in OUT_DIR, which render.rs inlines with include_str!. The page therefore has exactly one classic <script>, needs no module loader and resolves nothing at runtime.
  • Which esbuild. node_modules/esbuild/bin/esbuild is not one kind of file: a Windows install keeps the JavaScript launcher there, while a POSIX install links the native executable of the @esbuild/<os>-<cpu> package over the same path. build.rs therefore resolves the executable the way esbuild's own install script does (an explicit ESBUILD_BINARY_PATH, then the platform package, then the installer's download, then the launcher) and executes a native binary directly, falling back to node only for a real script, so the ELF file a POSIX install leaves at the launcher path is never fed to node.
  • Dependencies. Third-party JavaScript is ordinary npm, with exact versions in package.json and bytes pinned by package-lock.json. npm ci is a build prerequisite; a missing dependency fails the build with an actionable message instead of degrading silently.
  • Chapter folding is a declared option of the shared body. doc-body.js owns both halves of a whole-document render, and each is the caller's declaration rather than the module's guess: the article enhances its tables and folds its chapters, the hover preview enhances the tables and folds nothing, and the search preview does neither — the filter panel would be read as a press outside the dialog, and a fold arrow inside it would answer a click that already belongs to the list. Chapters are taken from the rendered DOM, not from the payload's outline, so a heading an author wrote as raw HTML is foldable too; a chapter runs to the next heading of the same or a higher level, so folding one covers everything nested under it. The fold state lives in the DOM alone (aria-expanded, hidden) and is never stored, so a body rebuilt for another document opens whole; a navigation into a folded chapter reopens the chapters that hold it before scrolling, because nothing scrolls to a hidden element.
  • Math is typeset by the bundled KaTeX. The build emits the LaTeX source of $$…$$ blocks and $…$ spans as placeholder elements (pre.math, code.math-inline), and the reader typesets them with the engine after insertion — the same insertion-time contract as the diagrams, though the math engine needs no layout. The engine's stylesheet is staged by build.rs with every font embedded as a data URL, so the offline guarantee holds. Colours are inherited from the text, so a theme switch needs no re-render, and a formula that fails to typeset keeps its source text.
  • Documents are looked up, then fetched. doc-store.js is the one place that knows where a document's model comes from: the payload for the shell formats, a pages/<id>.json file for the pages format. The controller renders from the store's peek when the document is on hand — every navigation of the shell formats, any revisit of the split one — and awaits get otherwise, showing a loading note and dropping the answer when a newer navigation has taken the article over. The views that need another document (the hover preview, the search panel's whole-document preview) take the store, answer synchronously from peek, and fall back to get. The search corpus of the split format is fetched once, on the first global search; the local scope reads the document in view, which is already in hand, so the default scope costs nothing.
  • The opening document. router.js resolves the address with one fallback chain: a known id, then the site's configured home (the payload's home key, honoured only when it names a known document), then the first document. Explicit links are never redirected; the setting only decides what an empty or unknown address opens.
  • Layering rule. Pure logic and DOM access live in separate modules (router.js, links.js, asset-links.js, search.js, doc-store.js, table.js, graph.js, preview.js, toc.js, anchor.js, diagrams.js, math.js versus table-view.js, graph-view.js, diagram-view.js, math-view.js, preview-view.js, search-view.js, search-highlight.js, banner.js, doc-list.js), because the JS test suite runs under node --test with no DOM. Anything that touches document belongs to a view module; a view is a projection of the pure functions beneath it, and the controller (app.js) is the only module that wires views to the payload and the router.
  • No UI framework. The reader stays on native DOM. The interactive surface is one popover plus a few attribute toggles, which does not pay for a component runtime: a framework bundle would fight the single-inline-classic- script requirement, add an output layer to the byte-identical bundle and force a DOM test environment on logic that is otherwise covered by node --test. esbuild and plain ES modules stay the whole front-end build chain.
  • Gesture state belongs to the module that takes it. A press is recorded by the module that saw it, because the browsers and the d3 behaviours cancel every press they take, so a cancellation says nothing about ownership. A press is only ended early by a window that no longer holds the focus.
  • One CSS custom-property set per theme. Light and dark are one declaration block switched by a root attribute; the toggle changes no other state.

8. Testing

LayerLocationToolingCovers
Rust unit#[cfg(test)] in each modulecargo test --libslugs, TOC, links, assets, highlighting, render, writers, options, pipeline, config, error mapping
Rust integrationtests/*.rsassert_cmd, tempfile, predicatesCLI, scan, config, markdown, writers, end to end, the esbuild launcher build.rs picks
Front-end unittests/js/*.test.jsnode --test, node:assertrouter, search, table model, graph layout, outline, preview, banner, inlined links, math policy
Bridgetests/js_suite.rsCommand::new("node")runs the JS suite inside cargo test

Fixtures under tests/fixtures are committed sites, each pinned to one class of input; no test touches the network. The front-end dependencies are installed once with npm ci and the tests only read node_modules.

Quality gates for any change: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, npm run check and cargo test must all pass.

9. Constraints and risks

ConstraintImpactMitigation
Embedded diagram engine dominates the bundleevery format carries itminification plus a size guard; the engine is only initialised when the current document has a diagram
Front-end dependencies are installed outside Cargocargo build needs npm ci firstbuild.rs fails with an actionable message; versions and bytes are pinned
The npm esbuild launcher is a script on Windows and a native binary elsewhererunning the launcher path through node fails on POSIXbuild.rs resolves the executable and starts a script with node only; a native binary runs directly
file:// restrictions (CORS, module scripts)a naive SPA would breakthe shell formats inline the payload; the pages format requires an HTTP host and says so on a file:// page
Large media in memorypeak RAM during base64 encodingsingle-pass placeholder expansion into one reused buffer, so peak memory is the page plus one asset
Raw HTML passthroughXSS if untrusted Markdown is compileddocumented as trusted-input behaviour; no sanitizer
No incremental buildfull rebuild on every runacceptable at folder scale; the artifacts are deterministic
The Windows icon is a derived assetdocs/logo.svg and docs/logo.ico can drift apartthe icon is rendered from the source and committed, and tools/make-icon.mjs packs it deterministically; regenerating it after a design change is a documented manual step

Chapters are taken from the rendered DOM, not from the payload's outline, so a heading an author wrote as raw HTML is foldable too; a chapter runs to the next heading of the same or a higher level, so folding one covers everything nested under it. The fold state lives in the DOM alone (aria-expanded, hidden) and is never stored, so a body rebuilt for another document opens whole; a navigation into a folded chapter reopens the chapters that hold it before scrolling, because nothing scrolls to a hidden element.
  • Math is typeset by the bundled KaTeX. The build emits the LaTeX source of $$…$$ blocks and $…$ spans as placeholder elements (pre.math, code.math-inline), and the reader typesets them with the engine after insertion — the same insertion-time contract as the diagrams, though the math engine needs no layout. The engine's stylesheet is staged by build.rs with every font embedded as a data URL, so the offline guarantee holds. Colours are inherited from the text, so a theme switch needs no re-render, and a formula that fails to typeset keeps its source text.
  • Documents are looked up, then fetched. doc-store.js is the one place that knows where a document's model comes from: the payload for the shell formats, a pages/<id>.json file for the pages format. The controller renders from the store's peek when the document is on hand — every navigation of the shell formats, any revisit of the split one — and awaits get otherwise, showing a loading note and dropping the answer when a newer navigation has taken the article over. The views that need another document (the hover preview, the search panel's whole-document preview) take the store, answer synchronously from peek, and fall back to get. The search corpus of the split format is fetched once, on the first global search; the local scope reads the document in view, which is already in hand, so the default scope costs nothing.
  • The opening document. router.js resolves the address with one fallback chain: a known id, then the site's configured home (the payload's home key, honoured only when it names a known document), then the first document. Explicit links are never redirected; the setting only decides what an empty or unknown address opens.
  • Layering rule. Pure logic and DOM access live in separate modules (router.js, links.js, asset-links.js, search.js, doc-store.js, table.js, graph.js, preview.js, toc.js, anchor.js, diagrams.js, math.js versus table-view.js, graph-view.js, diagram-view.js, math-view.js, preview-view.js, search-view.js, search-highlight.js, banner.js, doc-list.js), because the JS test suite runs under node --test with no DOM. Anything that touches document belongs to a view module; a view is a projection of the pure functions beneath it, and the controller (app.js) is the only module that wires views to the payload and the router.
  • No UI framework. The reader stays on native DOM. The interactive surface is one popover plus a few attribute toggles, which does not pay for a component runtime: a framework bundle would fight the single-inline-classic- script requirement, add an output layer to the byte-identical bundle and force a DOM test environment on logic that is otherwise covered by node --test. esbuild and plain ES modules stay the whole front-end build chain.
  • Gesture state belongs to the module that takes it. A press is recorded by the module that saw it, because the browsers and the d3 behaviours cancel every press they take, so a cancellation says nothing about ownership. A press is only ended early by a window that no longer holds the focus.
  • One CSS custom-property set per theme. Light and dark are one declaration block switched by a root attribute; the toggle changes no other state.

8. Testing

LayerLocationToolingCovers
Rust unit#[cfg(test)] in each modulecargo test --libslugs, TOC, links, assets, highlighting, render, writers, options, pipeline, config, error mapping
Rust integrationtests/*.rsassert_cmd, tempfile, predicatesCLI, scan, config, markdown, writers, end to end, the esbuild launcher build.rs picks
Front-end unittests/js/*.test.jsnode --test, node:assertrouter, search, table model, graph layout, outline, preview, banner, inlined links, math policy
Bridgetests/js_suite.rsCommand::new("node")runs the JS suite inside cargo test

Fixtures under tests/fixtures are committed sites, each pinned to one class of input; no test touches the network. The front-end dependencies are installed once with npm ci and the tests only read node_modules.

text: wikicc — Architecture This document describes how wikicc is built: its layers, the direction of their dependencies, the invariants the stages must keep, and the constraints that shape them. It deliberately stays at that level — product behaviour is described in README.md, and per-stage implementation details live in the code. 1. Shape of the system wikicc is one Rust binary plus one embedded front-end bundle. The binary owns everything that can be decided at build time; the bundle owns everything that has to happen in the reader. They communicate through exactly one channel: a JSON payload embedded in the page. build time │ run time │ input dir ──▶ pipeline stages ──▶ artifact │ artifact ──▶ reader modules (Rust: scan, parse, resolve, │ (ES modules bundled by assemble, render, write) │ esbuild, inlined as one │ classic script) payload (JSON) ─┼─▶ Nothing is resolved at run time across the boundary: the bundle knows its imports when it is built, and the payload is already on the page when the script runs. There is no server in either half. 2. Pipeline scan ──▶ parse ──▶ resolve ──▶ assemble ──▶ render ──▶ write .md HTML + link/asset SiteBundle page or 3 formats files TOC + rewriting, (JSON) page + via highlight asset bytes chunks SiteWriter pipeline::run owns the order and the side effects: Stage Input → output Module validate raw arguments + .wikicc.json → merged, guarded Options cli, options, config config input root → optional .wikicc.json → SiteConfig config scan directory + Options.exclude → ScanReport scan parse SourceDoc → HTML, TOC, plain text markdown resolve destinations → final addressing, AssetTable, diagnostics markdown::links, assets assemble everything → SiteBundle + SiteBuild site render SiteBundle → the shell page, or the shell plus one chunk per document and the search corpus render write RenderedOutput + SiteBuild → files writers Every stage except write is a pure transformation over immutable data, so it is unit tested without a filesystem. The order of the side effects is part of the contract: diagnostics are reported first, then the --strict gate runs, and only then is the page rendered and written. A build that fails on warnings therefore neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one. 3. Module map src/main.rs binary: parse arguments, dispatch --init-config, run the pipeline, map errors to exit codes src/lib.rs library root and re-exports src/cli.rs clap definitions src/options.rs the shared Settings of the CLI and the configuration file, the CLI-over-file merge, defaults, path guards src/error.rs error type and exit-code mapping src/pipeline.rs stage order, strict gate, summary lines src/scan.rs discovery, ordering, ids, titles, diagnostics src/config.rs the optional `.wikicc.json` site configuration and its initializer src/markdown/ render orchestration, heading text, slugs, TOC, chapter blocks, highlighting, link resolution, reference definitions src/assets.rs read, MIME, hashing, dedupe src/site.rs payload types and assembly src/render.rs shell assembly (template, CSS, script, payload), size guard src/writers/ one writer per format plus the shared placeholder expansion src/web/ page template, stylesheet and the reader's ES modules build.rs bundles src/web/js/main.js with esbuild into OUT_DIR, and embeds docs/logo.ico into the Windows executable tools/make-icon.mjs packs the rendered icon sizes into docs/logo.ico Dependency direction is one-way: cli → options → scan → markdown → site → render → writers → pipeline. config reads only its own file and imports options (the shared Settings) and scan (the diagnostic type), so it feeds the scan without anything reaching back into it. markdown::links never depends on site, so link resolution stays testable on its own. 4. Invariants Rewrite the tree, not the HTML. Every document is parsed once with markdown-rs into mdast, converted to the own-layer tree, and passed through the own-layer transforms (citation fold, wikilinks, inline sugar, lenient spaced destinations, callouts) before the serialiser runs. Link and image destinations are rewritten structurally while that serialiser emits elements. Regex post-processing of HTML is rejected because attribute quoting and nesting make it unsound. One page, two addressing schemes. The document HTML is rendered once and carries an opaque placeholder (wikicc-asset:<hash>) wherever a local resource is referenced. Writers expand the placeholder into the addressing form of their format. The placeholder only ever appears inside the JSON payload, and every substitution value is quote-free, so the payload stays valid JSON. The shell formats inline the payload; the pages format fetches. single-html and html-dir must work over file://, where fetch() of a local JSON file is blocked by CORS, so their whole payload is embedded in the page. pages is an artifact for an HTTP host: its page embeds only the manifest — one {id, title, hash} reference per document — and each document's model is one JSON file under pages/ that the reader fetches when it navigates there, with the search corpus in search.json fetched on the first global search. That format does not open from file://, and the reader says so when it finds itself there. Chunk file names derive from the document id alone, so a cached page never points at a file a redeploy removed; freshness travels in the hash, appended as a ?v= query a static host ignores but a browser counts as a new address. Assets are content-addressed. The name is the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 digest plus the original extension, which gives free deduplication and stable names across builds and platforms. Fail soft by default. Broken links and missing assets become warnings and the original destination is left untouched; --strict upgrades them to a non-zero exit. Raw HTML passes through unchanged. The input is trusted (a local documentation folder); there is no sanitizer in this version, and this is documented rather than half-implemented. A block ends at the next heading of any level. Each body is cut into blocks — one per heading, ending where the next heading of any level starts — so every paragraph is serialised exactly once. The outline is carried on the blocks themselves (parent, subtree), which keeps aggregation a lookup rather than a walk without repeating a paragraph under every ancestor. tests/e2e.rs asserts both halves: joining a root subtree reproduces doc.html exactly, and block markup costs one body copy however deep the outline goes. Heading text has one implementation. Anchors are matched during resolution, before the target document is rendered, so the pre-pass and the renderer build heading text through the same HeadingText accumulator and the same Slugger. A chapter the build accepts is therefore a chapter the reader can reach, and the route carries the emitted slug, since only that is an element id. Static state travels in the markup. Anything the reader must know about a link that the route grammar cannot express is written into the document as data-* attributes, and every consumer reads it from there. The mark goes on an inline <span hidden> immediately before the link — the shape that stays valid inside a paragraph, a list item or a table cell, and the one the reader copies onto the anchor it points at. 5. Determinism Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts. This is a hard requirement, not an aspiration, and it constrains every stage: documents are ordered by relative path in byte order; collections that reach the output are BTreeMap/BTreeSet or explicitly sorted; assets are named after their content hash, so duplicates collapse and names do not depend on discovery order; no artifact contains a timestamp, an absolute path, a host name or a random value. The elapsed time exists only in the stdout summary; on the front end, the force layout is seeded from a hash of the document ids, the same generator feeds the initial jitter and simulation.randomSource(), and the simulation is stepped synchronously. 6. Contracts at the edges These are the boundaries where an internal change becomes observable, so each one is stated as a contract rather than left to the implementation. The configuration file. .wikicc.json sits in the input folder root and is optional. It carries six keys — home, exclude, out, format, title, strict — exactly the Settings shape the command line also expresses, and every value it names is a default the command line overrides. A relative out is resolved against the input folder (the folder the file sits in), so the build lands in the same place whatever the working directory. The file is read once, before the scan (the exclude entries must be in effect while the tree is walked; resolving home still waits for the document ids), and parsing is strict: an unreadable or unparseable file is a runtime failure, while a home that matches no document and an unknown key are warnings the --strict gate counts. The resolved id travels in the payload as home and in the pages manifest under the same key, omitted when unset, so a site without the file serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of it. exclude lists directories relative to the input folder that are pruned with their subtrees; the pruned directories are reported as a note line, and an entry that escapes the input folder is a runtime failure, whatever the source it came from. A starter file is written by wikicc --init-config [DIR]: the default content (every key unset) goes into a directory that already exists, and a file that is already there is never overwritten. CLI surface. cli defines the arguments; options owns the shared Settings (the shape both the command line and the configuration file express), merges the command line over the file over the built-in defaults into Options, and owns the output-directory guards (missing and empty are used, a previous artifact is emptied, anything else needs --force, and the output directory may not be the input root, its ancestor or the working directory). Three combinations are rejected before anything is written. --home and a repeatable --exclude replace the configured values, and --strict is three-state: a bare flag turns the gate on, --strict=false turns it off. Exit codes. error maps every failure to 0 (success, possibly with warnings), 1 (runtime failure, including --strict with warnings) or 2 (usage error, reported by clap). The mapping is centralised so a new stage cannot invent a code. Streams. Diagnostics go to stderr, the summary line to stdout (unless --quiet). The summary names counts, output directory, format and elapsed time — never a value that ends up inside an artifact. Testability. Everything the run prints goes through a std::io::Write sink rather than println!, so wording, gate and --quiet are unit tested without spawning a process. Formats. The three writers never re-render markup: the two shell writers share the page and differ only in asset addressing, and the pages writer expands the same placeholders into its chunk files. A writer receives the render of its own format and refuses any other. The pages writer expands every chunk before it writes anything, writes the shell page last, so the artifact never references a file that is not on disk, and an asset-free or document-free site writes no empty directory. Weight. render.rs holds a size guard that fails the build if the bundle regresses. The Windows icon. A Windows executable shows an icon in the file explorer, and that icon lives in the PE resource section. docs/logo.svg is the design source; docs/logo.ico is rendered from it and committed, so the build needs no image toolchain and stays reproducible. build.rs compiles the icon into the executable for Windows targets only, and every other target produces exactly the binary it produced before.
